claim: A predominantly fish-eating diet was envisioned for Spinosaurus aegyptiacus when its elongate jaws with subconical teeth were unearthed a century ago in Egypt.
source: A predominantly fish-eating diet was envisioned for the sail-backed theropod dinosaur Spinosaurus aegyptiacus when its elongate jaws with subconical teeth were unearthed a century ago in Egypt.
evidence: This claim is supported by historical citation to the original discovery and interpretation of the fossil.

claim: Recent discovery of the high-spined tail of the neotypic skeleton led to the conjecture that S. aegyptiacus was the first fully aquatic dinosaur.
source: Recent discovery of the high-spined tail of that skeleton, however, led to a bolder conjecture that S. aegyptiacus was the first fully aquatic dinosaur.
evidence: This claim references recent discoveries and the resulting hypothesis proposed by other researchers.

claim: The 'aquatic hypothesis' posits that S. aegyptiacus was a slow quadruped on land.
source: The 'aquatic hypothesis' posits that S. aegyptiacus was a slow quadruped on land but a capable pursuit predator in coastal waters, powered by an expanded tail.
evidence: This is a statement of what the aquatic hypothesis proposes, as described by other researchers.

claim: The 'aquatic hypothesis' posits that S. aegyptiacus was a capable pursuit predator in coastal waters, powered by an expanded tail.
source: The 'aquatic hypothesis' posits that S. aegyptiacus was a slow quadruped on land but a capable pursuit predator in coastal waters, powered by an expanded tail.
evidence: This is a statement of what the aquatic hypothesis proposes, as described by other researchers.

claim: On land S. aegyptiacus was bipedal.
source: That model shows that on land S. aegyptiacus was bipedal and in deep water was an unstable, slow-surface swimmer (<1 m/s) too buoyant to dive.
evidence: This claim is supported by biomechanical modeling and center of mass calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: In deep water S. aegyptiacus was an unstable, slow-surface swimmer with speed less than 1 m/s.
source: That model shows that on land S. aegyptiacus was bipedal and in deep water was an unstable, slow-surface swimmer (<1 m/s) too buoyant to dive.
evidence: This claim is supported by biomechanical calculations of swimming velocity and stability presented in the manuscript.

claim: S. aegyptiacus was too buoyant to dive.
source: That model shows that on land S. aegyptiacus was bipedal and in deep water was an unstable, slow-surface swimmer (<1 m/s) too buoyant to dive.
evidence: This claim is supported by buoyancy calculations and biomechanical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Living reptiles with similar spine-supported sails over trunk and tail are used for display rather than aquatic propulsion.
source: Living reptiles with similar spine-supported sails over trunk and tail are used for display rather than aquatic propulsion, and nearly all extant secondary swimmers have reduced limbs and fleshy tail flukes.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis with extant reptiles presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nearly all extant secondary swimmers have reduced limbs and fleshy tail flukes.
source: Living reptiles with similar spine-supported sails over trunk and tail are used for display rather than aquatic propulsion, and nearly all extant secondary swimmers have reduced limbs and fleshy tail flukes.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis with extant secondary swimmers and established knowledge of aquatic adaptations.

claim: New fossils show that Spinosaurus ranged far inland.
source: New fossils also show that Spinosaurus ranged far inland.
evidence: This claim is supported by new fossil discoveries from inland sites in Niger described in the manuscript.

claim: Spinosaurus is best understood as a semiaquatic bipedal ambush piscivore that frequented the margins of coastal and inland waterways.
source: Two stages are clarified in the evolution of Spinosaurus, which is best understood as a semiaquatic bipedal ambush piscivore that frequented the margins of coastal and inland waterways.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by multiple lines of evidence including biomechanical analysis, comparative anatomy, and fossil distribution.

claim: Ernst von Stromer announced the discovery of Spinosaurus aegyptiacus in 1915.
source: In 1915, Ernst von Stromer announced the discovery in Egypt's Western Desert of the elongate jaws and partial skeleton of a large sail-backed predator Spinosaurus aegyptiacus (Stromer, 1915).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to the original publication.

claim: Stromer's initial reconstruction of S. aegyptiacus was as a sail-backed, piscivorous biped.
source: Other bones found nearby (Stromer, 1934) contributed to his initial reconstruction of S. aegyptiacus as a sail-backed, piscivorous biped (Stromer, 1936), shortly before all of these bones were destroyed in World War II (Nothdurft et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stromer's original work.

claim: All of Stromer's Spinosaurus bones were destroyed in World War II.
source: Other bones found nearby (Stromer, 1934) contributed to his initial reconstruction of S. aegyptiacus as a sail-backed, piscivorous biped (Stromer, 1936), shortly before all of these bones were destroyed in World War II (Nothdurft et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations.

claim: Additional skull and postcranial bones of Spinosaurus came to light in western Morocco over the last 30 years.
source: Over the last 30 years, additional skull and postcranial bones came to light in western Morocco in beds of similar age to those in Egypt (Russell, 1996; Dal Sasso et al., 2005; Smyth et al., 2020; Ibrahim et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to fossil discoveries.

claim: A partial skeleton designated as the neotype allowed a more complete reconstruction of S. aegyptiacus, confirming its interpretation as a semiaquatic piscivore.
source: Central among these finds was a partial skeleton (designated the neotype) that allowed a more complete reconstruction, confirming its interpretation as a semiaquatic piscivore (Ibrahim et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the neotype description.

claim: Oxygen isotopes in enamel have been used to infer that S. aegyptiacus was better adapted to life in water as an aquatic predator.
source: As skeletal information on the unusual predator improved, so has speculation as to whether S. aegyptiacus was better adapted to life in water as an aquatic predator, based on inferences from oxygen isotopes in enamel (Amiot et al., 2010), the dental rosette likened to the jaws of a conger eel (Vullo et al., 2016), the alleged elevated positioning of the orbits in the skull for visibility while largely submerged (Arden et al., 2019), the hypothetical underwater role of the trunk sail (Gimsa et al., 2016), and the infilling of the medullary cavities of hind limb bones that may have functioned as ballast (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Aureliano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references interpretations made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The dental rosette of S. aegyptiacus has been likened to the jaws of a conger eel.
source: As skeletal information on the unusual predator improved, so has speculation as to whether S. aegyptiacus was better adapted to life in water as an aquatic predator, based on inferences from oxygen isotopes in enamel (Amiot et al., 2010), the dental rosette likened to the jaws of a conger eel (Vullo et al., 2016), the alleged elevated positioning of the orbits in the skull for visibility while largely submerged (Arden et al., 2019), the hypothetical underwater role of the trunk sail (Gimsa et al., 2016), and the infilling of the medullary cavities of hind limb bones that may have functioned as ballast (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Aureliano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references an interpretation made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The orbits in the skull of S. aegyptiacus have been alleged to be elevated for visibility while largely submerged.
source: As skeletal information on the unusual predator improved, so has speculation as to whether S. aegyptiacus was better adapted to life in water as an aquatic predator, based on inferences from oxygen isotopes in enamel (Amiot et al., 2010), the dental rosette likened to the jaws of a conger eel (Vullo et al., 2016), the alleged elevated positioning of the orbits in the skull for visibility while largely submerged (Arden et al., 2019), the hypothetical underwater role of the trunk sail (Gimsa et al., 2016), and the infilling of the medullary cavities of hind limb bones that may have functioned as ballast (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Aureliano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references an interpretation made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The trunk sail of S. aegyptiacus has been hypothesized to have an underwater role.
source: As skeletal information on the unusual predator improved, so has speculation as to whether S. aegyptiacus was better adapted to life in water as an aquatic predator, based on inferences from oxygen isotopes in enamel (Amiot et al., 2010), the dental rosette likened to the jaws of a conger eel (Vullo et al., 2016), the alleged elevated positioning of the orbits in the skull for visibility while largely submerged (Arden et al., 2019), the hypothetical underwater role of the trunk sail (Gimsa et al., 2016), and the infilling of the medullary cavities of hind limb bones that may have functioned as ballast (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Aureliano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The infilling of the medullary cavities of hind limb bones in S. aegyptiacus may have functioned as ballast.
source: As skeletal information on the unusual predator improved, so has speculation as to whether S. aegyptiacus was better adapted to life in water as an aquatic predator, based on inferences from oxygen isotopes in enamel (Amiot et al., 2010), the dental rosette likened to the jaws of a conger eel (Vullo et al., 2016), the alleged elevated positioning of the orbits in the skull for visibility while largely submerged (Arden et al., 2019), the hypothetical underwater role of the trunk sail (Gimsa et al., 2016), and the infilling of the medullary cavities of hind limb bones that may have functioned as ballast (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Aureliano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references an interpretation made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: Recent discovery of the tall-spined tail bones of the neotypic skeleton reinvigorated the interpretation of S. aegyptiacus as the first fully aquatic dinosaur.
source: Recent discovery of the tall-spined tail bones of the neotypic skeleton reinvigorated the interpretation of S. aegyptiacus as the first fully aquatic dinosaur (Ibrahim et al., 2020b), here dubbed the 'aquatic hypothesis,' which makes three basic propositions.
evidence: This claim references the aquatic hypothesis proposed by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The propulsive capacity of the tail in water was judged to be better than terrestrial counterparts by oscillating miniature plastic tail cutouts in water.
source: The propulsive capacity of the tail in water was judged to be better than terrestrial counterparts by oscillating miniature plastic tail cutouts in water (Ibrahim et al., 2020b), a limited approximation of the biomechanical properties of an anguilliform tail (Lighthill, 1969; van Rees et al., 2013; Gutarra and Rahman, 2022) that failed to take account of the bizarre anterior half of the animal.
evidence: This claim describes experimental methods used by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The center of body mass has been estimated for S. aegyptiacus three times, each estimate pointing to a different location ranging from the middle of the trunk to a position over the hind limbs.
source: The center of body mass, a critical functional parameter, has been estimated for S. aegyptiacus three times, each estimate pointing to a different location ranging from the middle of the trunk (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Ibrahim et al., 2020b) to a position over the hind limbs (Henderson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that calculated center of mass.

claim: Adequate evaluation of the aquatic hypothesis requires more realistic biomechanical tests.
source: Thus, adequate evaluation of the aquatic hypothesis requires more realistic biomechanical tests, quantitative body, axial and limb comparisons between S. aegyptiacus and extant primary and secondary swimmers, and a survey of bone structure beyond the femur and shaft of a dorsal rib.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' methodological approach and reasoning.

claim: An accurate 3D digital flesh model of S. aegyptiacus requires an accurate skeletal model.
source: Such tests and comparisons require an accurate 3D digital flesh model of S. aegyptiacus, which, in turn, requires an accurate skeletal model.
evidence: This is a logical statement about methodological requirements.

claim: A complete set of CT scans of the fossil bones for S. aegyptiacus and its African forerunner, Suchomimus tenerensis, were assembled for this study.
source: Hence, we began this study by assembling a complete set of CT scans of the fossil bones for S. aegyptiacus and its African forerunner, Suchomimus tenerensis (Sereno et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes the data collection methods used in the study.

claim: The hypothesis holds that S. aegyptiacus was not only a diving pursuit predator in the open-water column, but also a quadruped on land with long-clawed forelimbs poorly adapted for weight support.
source: The contention is that S. aegyptiacus was not only a diving pursuit predator in the open-water column, but also a quadruped on land with long-clawed forelimbs poorly adapted for weight support.
evidence: This describes the aquatic hypothesis proposed by other researchers.

claim: A later publication seemed to downgrade the central claim of the aquatic hypothesis by suggesting that any vertebrate with 'aquatic habits,' such as wading, submergence, or diving, had an 'aquatic lifestyle'.
source: A later publication seemed to downgrade that central claim by suggesting that any vertebrate with 'aquatic habits,' such as wading, submergence, or diving, had an 'aquatic lifestyle' (Fabbri et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes a shift in terminology used by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: A vertebrate with an 'aquatic lifestyle' or 'aquatic ecology' is adapted for life primarily, or solely, in water with severely reduced functional capacity on land.
source: In the former case, a vertebrate with an 'aquatic lifestyle' or 'aquatic ecology' is adapted for life primarily, or solely, in water with severely reduced functional capacity on land (Pacini and Harper, 2008).
evidence: This is a definition based on established terminology in the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Aquatic vertebrates live exclusively or primarily in water and exhibit profound cranial, axial, or appendicular modifications for life in water, especially at larger body sizes.
source: Aquatic vertebrates (e.g., bony fish, sea turtles, whales) live exclusively or primarily in water and exhibit profound cranial, axial, or appendicular modifications for life in water, especially at larger body sizes (Webb, 1984; Webb and De Buffrénil, 1990; Hood, 2020).
evidence: This is a general statement about aquatic vertebrates supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Extant whales are secondarily aquatic mammals that spend all of their lives at sea and exhibit profound skeletal modifications for aquatic sensory and locomotor function.
source: For example, extant whales are secondarily aquatic mammals that spend all of their lives at sea and exhibit profound skeletal modifications for aquatic sensory and locomotor function.
evidence: This is an example based on established knowledge of whale biology.

claim: A marine turtle is considered an aquatic reptile, regardless of whether it ventures ashore briefly to lay eggs, because the vast majority of its life is spent in water using profoundly modified limbs for aquatic locomotion.
source: A marine turtle, similarly, is considered an aquatic reptile, regardless of whether it ventures ashore briefly to lay eggs, because the vast majority of its life is spent in water using profoundly modified limbs for aquatic locomotion (flippers) that function poorly on land.
evidence: This is an example based on established knowledge of marine turtle biology.

claim: Nearly all semiaquatic vertebrates are secondarily aquaphilic, having acquired aquatic adaptations over time to enhance functional capacity in water without seriously compromising terrestrial function.
source: Nearly all semiaquatic vertebrates are secondarily aquaphilic, having acquired aquatic adaptations over time to enhance functional capacity in water without seriously compromising terrestrial function (Howell, 1930; Hood, 2020).
evidence: This is a general statement about semiaquatic vertebrates supported by citations.

claim: Semiaquatic animals are also semiterrestrial.
source: Indeed, semiaquatic animals are also semiterrestrial (Fish, 2016).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation.

claim: Freshwater turtles are regarded as semiaquatic reptiles because they frequent water rather than live exclusively within an aqueous habitat, are sometimes found in inland habitats, and exhibit an array of less profound modifications for locomotion in water.
source: For example, freshwater turtles are regarded as semiaquatic reptiles because they frequent water rather than live exclusively within an aqueous habitat, are sometimes found in inland habitats, and exhibit an array of less profound modifications (e.g., interdigital webbing) for locomotion in water (Pacini and Harper, 2008).
evidence: This is an example based on established knowledge of freshwater turtle biology, supported by citation.

claim: Extant crocodylians and many waterbirds are capable swimmers and divers but retain excellent functional capacity on land.
source: Likewise, extant crocodylians and many waterbirds are capable swimmers and divers but retain excellent functional capacity on land.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of crocodylian and waterbird biology.

claim: Auks are agile wing-propelled, pursuit divers with an awkward upright posture on land resembling penguins, but they retain the ability to fly and inhabit land for extended periods.
source: Auks (Alcidae), among the most water-adapted of semiaquatic avians, are agile wing-propelled, pursuit divers with an awkward upright posture on land resembling penguins, but they retain the ability to fly and inhabit land for extended periods (Nettleship, 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about auk biology supported by citation.

claim: Flightless penguins are considered aquatic due to their more profound skeletal modifications for swimming and deep diving and more limited terrestrial functionality.
source: On the other hand, the flightless penguins (Sphenisciformes) are considered aquatic due to their more profound skeletal modifications for swimming and deep diving and more limited terrestrial functionality, although still retaining the capacity to trek inland and stand for considerable durations while brooding.
evidence: This is a statement about penguin biology based on established knowledge.

claim: More profound functional allegiance to water is requisite for an 'aquatic' appellation.
source: As nearly all semiaquatic vertebrates have an aquatic diet and the ability to swim or dive, more profound functional allegiance to water is requisite for an 'aquatic' appellation (Pacini and Harper, 2008).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation.

claim: An aquatic adaptation of an organism refers to the function of a particular feature, not the overall lifestyle of an organism.
source: An aquatic adaptation of an organism refers to the function of a particular feature, not the overall lifestyle of an organism.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about terminology.

claim: An aquatic adaptation should have current utility and primary function in water.
source: That feature should have current utility and primary function in water (Houssaye and Fish, 2016).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation.

claim: Aquatic adaptations are presumed to have evolved their functionality in response to water and cannot also have special functional utility in a subaerial setting.
source: Aquatic adaptations are presumed to have evolved their functionality in response to water and cannot also have special functional utility in a subaerial setting.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the nature of aquatic adaptations.

claim: The downsized, retracted external nares in spinosaurids would inhibit water intake through the nostrils while feeding with the snout submerged.
source: For example, the downsized, retracted external nares in spinosaurids would inhibit water intake through the nostrils while feeding with the snout submerged (Sereno et al., 1998; Dal Sasso et al., 2005; Ibrahim et al., 2014; Hone and Holtz, 2021).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is at present no plausible alternative explanation involving terrestrial function for the downsizing and retraction of the external nares in spinosaurids.
source: There is at present no plausible alternative explanation involving terrestrial function for the downsizing and retraction of the external nares in spinosaurids, a unique condition among non-avian theropods.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and lack of alternative explanations.

claim: The downsizing and retraction of the external nares is a unique condition among non-avian theropods.
source: There is at present no plausible alternative explanation involving terrestrial function for the downsizing and retraction of the external nares in spinosaurids, a unique condition among non-avian theropods.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of theropod anatomy.

claim: The hypertrophied neural spines of the tail in S. aegyptiacus are ambiguous as an 'aquatic adaptation' because expanded tails can function both as aquatic propulsors and terrestrial display structures.
source: In contrast, the hypertrophied neural spines of the tail in S. aegyptiacus are ambiguous as an 'aquatic adaptation' because expanded tails can function both as aquatic propulsors and terrestrial display structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on functional considerations.

claim: The authors have not found substantiating evidence to interpret the heightened tail in S. aegyptiacus or other spinosaurids as an aquatic adaptation.
source: Using various comparative and biomechanical approaches (below), we have not found such substantiating evidence to interpret the heightened tail in S. aegyptiacus or other spinosaurids as an aquatic adaptation, confirming similar conclusions reached recently by Hone and Holtz, 2021.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analyses presented in the manuscript and supported by citation to similar conclusions.

claim: The skeletal reconstruction of adult S. aegyptiacus is just under 14 m long.
source: Our skeletal reconstruction of an adult S. aegyptiacus is just under 14 m long (Figure 1A), which is more than 1 m shorter than previously reported (Ibrahim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a measurement from the skeletal model created in this study, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The skeletal reconstruction of adult S. aegyptiacus is more than 1 m shorter than previously reported.
source: Our skeletal reconstruction of an adult S. aegyptiacus is just under 14 m long (Figure 1A), which is more than 1 m shorter than previously reported (Ibrahim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous estimates, supported by citation.

claim: The length of the presacral column in the 2D graphical reconstruction of the aquatic hypothesis was overestimated by approximately 10% over dimensions based on CT-scanned fossils.
source: The length of the presacral column, depth of the ribcage, and length of the forelimb in that reconstruction were overestimated by ~10, 25, and 30%, respectively, over dimensions based on CT-scanned fossils.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the authors' reconstruction and the aquatic hypothesis reconstruction.

claim: The depth of the ribcage in the 2D graphical reconstruction of the aquatic hypothesis was overestimated by approximately 25% over dimensions based on CT-scanned fossils.
source: The length of the presacral column, depth of the ribcage, and length of the forelimb in that reconstruction were overestimated by ~10, 25, and 30%, respectively, over dimensions based on CT-scanned fossils.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the authors' reconstruction and the aquatic hypothesis reconstruction.

claim: The length of the forelimb in the 2D graphical reconstruction of the aquatic hypothesis was overestimated by approximately 30% over dimensions based on CT-scanned fossils.
source: The length of the presacral column, depth of the ribcage, and length of the forelimb in that reconstruction were overestimated by ~10, 25, and 30%, respectively, over dimensions based on CT-scanned fossils.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the authors' reconstruction and the aquatic hypothesis reconstruction.

claim: All of the proportional overestimates in the aquatic hypothesis reconstruction shift the center of mass anteriorly when translated to a flesh model.
source: When translated to a flesh model, all of these proportional overestimates (heavier neck, trunk, forelimb) shift the center of mass anteriorly (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an inference about the biomechanical consequences of the dimensional differences.

claim: Cervical vertebrae in S. aegyptiacus contain large air-filled pneumatic spaces in the centra and neural arches.
source: Medullary space is present in most forelimb bones in both S. aegyptiacus and S. tenerensis (Figure 1D and H). The centra of anterior caudal vertebrae are occupied by a large medullary space (Figure 1C and J), and large air-filled pneumatic spaces are present in the centra and neural arches of cervical vertebrae (Evers et al., 2015; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from CT scans, shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation.

claim: The centra of anterior caudal vertebrae in S. aegyptiacus are occupied by a large medullary space.
source: Medullary space is present in most forelimb bones in both S. aegyptiacus and S. tenerensis (Figure 1D and H). The centra of anterior caudal vertebrae are occupied by a large medullary space (Figure 1C and J), and large air-filled pneumatic spaces are present in the centra and neural arches of cervical vertebrae (Evers et al., 2015; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from CT scans, shown in Figure 1C and J.

claim: Medullary space is present in most forelimb bones in both S. aegyptiacus and S. tenerensis.
source: Medullary space is present in most forelimb bones in both S. aegyptiacus and S. tenerensis (Figure 1D and H).
evidence: This is an observation from CT scans, shown in Figure 1D and H.

claim: The less dense, internal marrow- and air-filled spaces in S. aegyptiacus more than offset the added density of infilled medullary space in the relatively reduced hind limb long bones.
source: Collectively, these less dense, internal marrow- and air-filled spaces in S. aegyptiacus more than offset the added density of infilled medullary space in the relatively reduced hind limb long bones (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of air and marrow spaces observed in the fossils.

claim: Hind limb bone infilling is better explained as compensation for the reduced size of the hind limb long bones that must support a body mass at the upper end of the range for theropods.
source: Hind limb bone infilling is better explained as compensation for the reduced size of the hind limb long bones that must support a body mass at the upper end of the range for theropods.
evidence: This is an alternative functional interpretation proposed by the authors.

claim: Bending strength increases by as much as 35% when the medullary cavity is infilled.
source: Bending strength increases by as much as 35% when the medullary cavity is infilled (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a calculation presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The hind limb long bones in S. aegyptiacus lack the medullary cavity common to most dinosaurs and theropods in particular.
source: The hind limb long bones (femur, tibia, fibula, metatarsals) in S. aegyptiacus lack the medullary cavity common to most dinosaurs and theropods in particular.
evidence: This is an observation from the fossils compared to other dinosaurs.

claim: When first discovered, the infilled hind limb bones in S. aegyptiacus were interpreted as ballast for swimming.
source: When first discovered, the infilled hind limb bones in S. aegyptiacus were interpreted as ballast for swimming (Ibrahim et al., 2014).
evidence: This references an interpretation made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: The infilled condition of hind limb bones is variable as shown by the narrow medullary cavity in a femur of another individual slightly larger than the neotype.
source: However, the infilled condition is variable as shown by the narrow medullary cavity in a femur of another individual slightly larger than the neotype (Russell, 1996; NMC 41869).
evidence: This is an observation from another specimen, supported by citation.

claim: The bone infilling in S. aegyptiacus is fibrolamellar and cancellous, similar to the infilled medullary cavities of other large-bodied terrestrial dinosaurs and mammals.
source: Furthermore, the bone infilling is fibrolamellar and cancellous, similar to the infilled medullary cavities of other large-bodied terrestrial dinosaurs (Vanderven et al., 2014) and mammals (Houssaye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citations.

claim: Dense pachystotic bone composes the solid and sometimes swollen bones of many secondarily aquatic vertebrates that use increased skeletal density as ballast.
source: In contrast, dense pachystotic bone composes the solid and sometimes swollen bones of many secondarily aquatic vertebrates that use increased skeletal density as ballast (Houssaye, 2009).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about aquatic vertebrates supported by citation.

claim: Muscle volume in the flesh model was guided by CT cross-sections from extant lizards, crocodylians, and birds.
source: Muscle volume was guided by CT cross-sections from extant lizards, crocodylians, and birds (Figure 2B), and internal air space (pharynx-trachea, lungs, paraxial air sacs) was modeled on lizard, crocodilian, and avian conditions (Figure 2C; see 'Materials and methods,' Appendix 2).
evidence: This describes the methodology for creating the flesh model, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Internal air space (pharynx-trachea, lungs, paraxial air sacs) was modeled on lizard, crocodilian, and avian conditions.
source: Muscle volume was guided by CT cross-sections from extant lizards, crocodylians, and birds (Figure 2B), and internal air space (pharynx-trachea, lungs, paraxial air sacs) was modeled on lizard, crocodilian, and avian conditions (Figure 2C; see 'Materials and methods,' Appendix 2).
evidence: This describes the methodology for creating the flesh model, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: No matter the included volume of internal air space, the center of mass is positioned over the ground contact of symmetrically positioned hind feet.
source: No matter the included volume of internal air space, CM is positioned over the ground contact of symmetrically positioned hind feet (Figure 1A, red cross).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical modeling, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: S. aegyptiacus had a bipedal stance on land as previously suggested.
source: Thus, S. aegyptiacus had a bipedal stance on land as previously suggested (Henderson, 2018), contrary to trunk-centered CM of the aquatic hypothesis (Ibrahim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the center of mass calculations, supported by citation to a previous study and contrasted with the aquatic hypothesis.

claim: The manus in S. aegyptiacus is adapted for prey capture and manipulation rather than weight support.
source: Consistent with a bipedal stance, the manus is adapted for prey capture and manipulation (elongate hollow phalanges, scythe-shaped unguals) rather than weight support (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the morphology of the manus shown in Figure 1A and D.

claim: Adult S. aegyptiacus can feed while standing in water with flotation occurring in water deeper than approximately 2.6 m.
source: Adult S. aegyptiacus can feed while standing in water with flotation occurring in water deeper than ~2.6 m (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical modeling, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In hybrid or axial swimming poses, trunk air space tilts the anterior end of the model upward.
source: In hybrid or axial swimming poses, trunk air space tilts the anterior end of the model upward (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical modeling, shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: With density-adjusted body partitions and avian-like internal air space, the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus has a body mass of 7390 kg and an average density of 833 kg/m3.
source: With density-adjusted body partitions and avian-like internal air space, the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus has a body mass of 7390 kg and an average density of 833 kg/m3 (see 'Materials and methods'), which is considerably less than the density of freshwater (1000 kg/m3) and saltwater (1026 kg/m3) or the average density of living crocodylians (1080 kg/m3; Grigg and Kirshner, 2015).
evidence: This is a calculation from the flesh model.

claim: The average density of the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus (833 kg/m3) is considerably less than the density of freshwater (1000 kg/m3) and saltwater (1026 kg/m3).
source: With density-adjusted body partitions and avian-like internal air space, the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus has a body mass of 7390 kg and an average density of 833 kg/m3 (see 'Materials and methods'), which is considerably less than the density of freshwater (1000 kg/m3) and saltwater (1026 kg/m3) or the average density of living crocodylians (1080 kg/m3; Grigg and Kirshner, 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of calculated density to known densities of water.

claim: The average density of living crocodylians is 1080 kg/m3.
source: With density-adjusted body partitions and avian-like internal air space, the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus has a body mass of 7390 kg and an average density of 833 kg/m3 (see 'Materials and methods'), which is considerably less than the density of freshwater (1000 kg/m3) and saltwater (1026 kg/m3) or the average density of living crocodylians (1080 kg/m3; Grigg and Kirshner, 2015).
evidence: This is a value from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Swimming velocity at the surface and underwater in extant lizards and crocodylians is powered by foot paddling and axial undulation (hybrid swimming) and at moderate to maximum speeds by axial undulation alone (axial swimming).
source: Swimming velocity at the surface and underwater in extant lizards and crocodylians is powered by foot paddling and axial undulation (hybrid swimming; Frey and Salisbury, 2001) and at moderate to maximum (critical) speeds by axial undulation alone (axial swimming) (Fish, 1984; Grigg and Kirshner, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about swimming modes in extant reptiles, supported by citations.

claim: Lighthill's bulk momentum formula was used to estimate maximum surface and underwater swimming velocity for the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus.
source: We used Lighthill's bulk momentum formula to estimate maximum surface and underwater swimming velocity for the flesh model of S. aegyptiacus (Lighthill, 1969).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for swimming velocity calculations, supported by citation.

claim: Maximum velocity at the surface for S. aegyptiacus is approximately 0.8 m/s.
source: The intersection of the thrust power curve and drag power curves, where the animal would be swimming at a constant velocity, indicates slow maximum velocity at the surface (~0.8 m/s) and only slightly greater when submerged (~1.4 m/s) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical calculations, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Maximum velocity when submerged for S. aegyptiacus is approximately 1.4 m/s.
source: The intersection of the thrust power curve and drag power curves, where the animal would be swimming at a constant velocity, indicates slow maximum velocity at the surface (~0.8 m/s) and only slightly greater when submerged (~1.4 m/s) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical calculations, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Maximum tail thrust in S. aegyptiacus is 820 Watts (683 N or 154 lbs), a relatively low value for the considerable caudal muscle mass in this large theropod.
source: Maximum tail thrust in S. aegyptiacus is 820 Watts (683 N or 154 lbs), a relatively low value for the considerable caudal muscle mass in this large theropod (Snively and Russell, 2007; Mallison et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical calculations, with comparison to muscle mass estimates supported by citations.

claim: Maximum velocity for S. aegyptiacus is only 1.2 m/s, an order of magnitude less than extant large-bodied pursuit predators.
source: As a result, maximum velocity is only 1.2 m/s, an order of magnitude less than extant large-bodied (>1 m) pursuit predators.
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical calculations compared to known velocities of extant predators.

claim: Extant large-bodied pursuit predators (mackerel sharks, billfish, dolphins, and killer whales) are capable of maximum velocities of 10–33 m/s.
source: These species (mackerel sharks, billfish, dolphins, and killer whales) are capable of maximum velocities of 10–33 m/s (Tinsley, 1984; Fish, 1998; Fish and Rohr, 1999; Iosilevskii and Weihs, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about swimming velocities in extant predators, supported by citations.

claim: When positioned upright in water, the trunk sail of S. aegyptiacus is emergent.
source: When positioned upright in water, the trunk sail of S. aegyptiacus is emergent (Figure 3B, position 1).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical modeling, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The flesh model of S. aegyptiacus is particularly susceptible to long-axis rotation given the proximity of CM and CB, with stable equilibrium attained when floating on its side.
source: The flesh model, however, is particularly susceptible to long-axis rotation given the proximity of CM and CB, with stable equilibrium attained when floating on its side (Figure 3B, position 3).
evidence: This is a result from the stability analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Righting in S. aegyptiacus requires substantial torque (~5000 Nm) that is impossible to generate with vertical limbs and a tail with far less maximum force output (~700 N).
source: Righting requires substantial torque (~5000 Nm) that is impossible to generate with vertical limbs and a tail with far less maximum force output (~700 N).
evidence: This is a result from the biomechanical calculations comparing required torque to available force.

claim: The stability predicament in S. aegyptiacus remains even with the smallest internal air space.
source: This stability predicament remains even with the smallest internal air space.
evidence: This is a result from testing different air space scenarios in the model.

claim: The absence of vertical stability and righting potential in water in S. aegyptiacus stands in stark contrast to the condition in extant crocodylians and marine mammals.
source: The absence of vertical stability and righting potential in water stands in stark contrast to the condition in extant crocodylians and marine mammals (Fish, 1998; Grigg and Kirshner, 2015).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations.

claim: Maneuverability in water wanes as body length increases.
source: Maneuverability in water (acceleration, turning radius, and speed) wanes as body length increases (Domenici, 2001; Parson et al., 2011; Domenici et al., 2014; Hirt et al., 2017; Gutarra and Rahman, 2022), which is further compromised in S. aegyptiacus by its rigid trunk (see below) and expansive, unretractable sail.
evidence: This is a general principle supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maneuverability in S. aegyptiacus is further compromised by its rigid trunk and expansive, unretractable sail.
source: Maneuverability in water (acceleration, turning radius, and speed) wanes as body length increases (Domenici, 2001; Parson et al., 2011; Domenici et al., 2014; Hirt et al., 2017; Gutarra and Rahman, 2022), which is further compromised in S. aegyptiacus by its rigid trunk (see below) and expansive, unretractable sail.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomy of S. aegyptiacus.

claim: Large-bodied secondary swimmers capable of pursuit predation in open water have fusiform body forms with a narrow caudal peduncle for efficient tail propulsion.
source: In contrast, large-bodied secondary swimmers capable of pursuit predation in open water have fusiform body forms with a narrow caudal peduncle for efficient tail propulsion (ichthyosaurs, cetaceans; Motani, 2009), control surfaces for reorientation, and narrow extensions (bills) to enhance velocity in close encounters with smaller more maneuverable prey (Maresh et al., 2004; Domenici et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about aquatic predators supported by citations.

claim: Besides some waterbirds, semiaquatic pursuit predators are rare and include only the small-bodied (<2 m), exceptionally maneuverable otters that employ undulatory swimming.
source: Besides some waterbirds, semiaquatic pursuit predators are rare and include only the small-bodied (<2 m), exceptionally maneuverable otters that employ undulatory swimming (Fish, 1994).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citation.

claim: Even with lizard-like internal air space, diving in S. aegyptiacus still requires approximately 15 times maximum force output of the tail.
source: Even with lizard-like internal air space, diving still requires ~15 times maximum force output of the tail.
evidence: This is a calculation based on an alternative air space scenario.

claim: To initiate a dive, the tail of S. aegyptiacus would be lifted into the air as the body rotates about CB, significantly reducing tail thrust.
source: To initiate a dive, furthermore, the tail would be lifted into the air as the body rotates about CB (Figure 2D), significantly reducing tail thrust.
evidence: This is an inference about diving mechanics based on the position of CB, illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: The common depictions of S. aegyptiacus as a diving underwater pursuit predator contradict a range of physical parameters and calculations.
source: The now common depictions of S. aegyptiacus as a diving underwater pursuit predator contradict a range of physical parameters and calculations, which collectively characterize this dinosaur as a slow, unstable, and awkward surface swimmer incapable of submergence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the biomechanical analyses presented.

claim: Axial flexibility is requisite for axial-propulsion in primary or secondary swimmers.
source: Axial flexibility is requisite for axial-propulsion in primary or secondary swimmers.
evidence: This is a general principle about swimming mechanics.

claim: In S. aegyptiacus, trunk and sacral vertebrae are immobilized by interlocking articulations (hyposphene-hypantrum), an expansive rigid dorsal sail composed of closely spaced neural spines, and fused sacral centra.
source: However, in S. aegyptiacus, trunk and sacral vertebrae are immobilized by interlocking articulations (hyposphene-hypantrum), an expansive rigid dorsal sail composed of closely spaced neural spines, and fused sacral centra (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the skeletal anatomy shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The caudal neural spines in S. aegyptiacus stiffen a bone-supported tail sail by an echelon of neural spines that cross several vertebral segments, which effectively resist bending at vertebral joints.
source: The caudal neural spines in S. aegyptiacus stiffen a bone-supported tail sail by an echelon of neural spines that cross several vertebral segments, which effectively resist bending at vertebral joints (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation and functional interpretation based on the anatomy shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The caudal centra in S. aegyptiacus have nearly uniform subquadrate proportions along the majority of the tail in lateral view, rather than narrowing, spool-shaped centra in crocodylians and other secondarily aquatic squamates.
source: The caudal centra in S. aegyptiacus have nearly uniform subquadrate proportions along the majority of the tail in lateral view, rather than narrowing, spool-shaped centra in crocodylians and other secondarily aquatic squamates (Figure 4D), which increases distal flexibility during tail undulation.
evidence: This is a comparative observation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The structural features of the tail in S. aegyptiacus suggest that it functioned more as a pliant billboard than flexible fluke.
source: These salient structural features of the tail suggest that it functioned more as a pliant billboard than flexible fluke.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the structural observations.

claim: No primary or secondary vertebrate swimmer has a comparable drag-magnifying, rigid dorsal sail including sailfish, the dorsal fin of which is fully retractable and composed of pliable spines in membrane.
source: No primary or secondary vertebrate swimmer has a comparable drag-magnifying, rigid dorsal sail including sailfish, the dorsal fin of which is fully retractable and composed of pliable spines in membrane (Domenici et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citation.

claim: The distal tail of secondary swimmers such as crocodylians, mosasaurs and cetaceans is expanded with pliable soft tissues free of bone to form a flexible caudal paddle or fluke.
source: In contrast, the distal tail of secondary swimmers such as crocodylians (Grigg and Kirshner, 2015), mosasaurs (Lindgren et al., 2013) and cetaceans (Fish, 1998) is expanded with pliable soft tissues free of bone to form a flexible caudal paddle or fluke (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Spine-supported, torso-to-caudal sails aligned with median cranial crests have evolved multiple times for intraspecific display rather than aquatic propulsion among extant lizards.
source: Spine-supported, torso-to-caudal sails aligned with median cranial crests, in contrast, have evolved multiple times for intraspecific display rather than aquatic propulsion among extant lizard (agamids, iguanians, chameleons).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on knowledge of extant lizard biology.

claim: Semiaquatic sailfin and basilisk lizards do not use their sails while swimming, spend very little time submerged, and are not aquatic pursuit predators.
source: Semiaquatic sailfin and basilisk lizards (Figure 4B), for example, do not use their sails while swimming, spend very little time submerged, and are not aquatic pursuit predators (Hone and Holtz, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about lizard behavior supported by citation and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Caudal centra proportions in most secondary swimmers grade from subquadrate to spool-shaped in the distal half of the tail to increase flexibility and undulatory amplitude.
source: Caudal centra proportions in most secondary swimmers, as mentioned above, grade from subquadrate to spool-shaped in the distal half of the tail to increase flexibility and undulatory amplitude (Figure 4D), whereas those in S. aegyptiacus maintain relatively uniform proportions along the tail.
evidence: This is a comparative statement shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The uniformity of subquadrate proportions in S. aegyptiacus should not be confused with a more derived piscine pattern of uniform, short, disc-shaped centra that has evolved in parallel in mosasaurs.
source: This uniformity of subquadrate proportions in S. aegyptiacus should not be confused with a more derived piscine pattern of uniform, short, disc-shaped centra that has evolved in parallel in mosasaurs (Lindgren et al., 2013; Figure 4D, Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a clarification about vertebral morphology supported by citation and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Appendage surface area in secondary swimmers is minimized to reduce drag because terrestrial limbs are inefficient aquatic propulsors.
source: Appendage (fore and hind limb) surface area in secondary swimmers is minimized to reduce drag because terrestrial limbs are inefficient aquatic propulsors.
evidence: This is a general principle about secondary swimmers.

claim: Appendage surface area in S. aegyptiacus is substantially greater than in reptilian and mammalian secondary swimmers and even exceeds that of the terrestrial predators Allosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
source: Appendage surface area in S. aegyptiacus, in contrast, is substantially greater than in reptilian and mammalian secondary swimmers and even exceeds that of the terrestrial predators Allosaurus and Tyrannosaurus (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 5.

claim: Interdigital webbing is used by some secondary swimmers to increase the area of the foot paddle.
source: Interdigital webbing is used by some secondary swimmers to increase the area of the foot paddle (Fish, 2004).
evidence: This is a general statement about secondary swimmers supported by citation.

claim: Extant crocodylians use their limbs in paddling only at launch and slow speed before tucking them against the body.
source: Extant crocodylians use their limbs in paddling only at launch and slow speed before tucking them against the body (Grigg and Kirshner, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about crocodylian swimming behavior supported by citation.

claim: Crocodylian interdigital webbing, which is better developed and always present in the hind foot, only modestly increases surface area (<20%).
source: Crocodylian interdigital webbing, which is better developed and always present in the hind foot (Figure 6C and D), only modestly increases surface area (<20%).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Crocodylian paddle area scales isometrically across a range of body size.
source: Across a range of body size, we show that crocodylian paddle area scales isometrically (Figure 6F; see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a result from scaling analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The crocodylian foot paddle becomes even less effective as a propulsor with increasing body size.
source: The crocodylian foot paddle, thus, becomes even less effective as a propulsor with increasing body size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scaling analysis.

claim: A crocodylian of spinosaurid size would have a foot paddle area an order of magnitude greater than is possible in S. aegyptiacus.
source: A crocodylian of spinosaurid size, nonetheless, would have a foot paddle area an order of magnitude greater than is possible in S. aegyptiacus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Even a fully webbed hind foot in S. aegyptiacus is far too small to have functioned either for significant aquatic propulsion or for stabilizing control.
source: Even a fully webbed hind foot in S. aegyptiacus (Figure 6A), for which there is no hard evidence to establish as likely, is far too small to have functioned either for significant aquatic propulsion or for stabilizing control.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on size comparisons shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Most Spinosaurus fossils come from marginal basins along northern Africa in deltaic sediment laid down during an early Late Cretaceous transgression.
source: Most Spinosaurus fossils come from marginal basins along northern Africa in deltaic sediment laid down during an early Late Cretaceous transgression (Figure 7A, sites 1, 2).
evidence: This is a statement about fossil distribution shown in Figure 7A.

claim: These deposits also include the majority of non-spinosaurid dinosaur remains, all of which may have been transported to some degree from inland habitats to coastal delta deposits.
source: These deposits, however, also include the majority of non-spinosaurid dinosaur remains, all of which may have been transported to some degree from inland habitats to coastal delta deposits.
evidence: This is an inference about taphonomy and fossil transport.

claim: Fossils pertaining to Spinosaurus were recently discovered in two inland basins in Niger far from a marine coastline.
source: We recently discovered fossils pertaining to Spinosaurus in two inland basins in Niger far from a marine coastline (Figure 7A, site 3).
evidence: This describes new fossil discoveries shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Spinosaurus fossils from inland Niger were buried in fluvial overbank deposits alongside terrestrial herbivores (rebbachisaurid and titanosaurian sauropods).
source: They were buried in fluvial overbank deposits alongside terrestrial herbivores (rebbachisaurid and titanosaurian sauropods) (see Appendix 4).
evidence: This describes the depositional context of the new fossils.

claim: The inland location of Spinosaurus fossils completely undermines the interpretation of S. aegyptiacus as a 'highly specialized aquatic predator that pursued and caught its prey in the water column'.
source: The inland location of these fossils completely undermines the interpretation of S. aegyptiacus as a 'highly specialized aquatic predator that pursued and caught its prey in the water column' (Ibrahim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the new fossil discoveries, contrasted with the aquatic hypothesis.

claim: All large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates are marine—both extant and extinct.
source: All large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates are marine—both extant (e.g., sea turtles, sirenians, seals, whales) and extinct (e.g., protostegid turtles, ichthyosaurs, metriorhynchoid crocodylomorphs, plesiosaurs).
evidence: This is a general statement about aquatic vertebrates based on established knowledge.

claim: None of the diverse large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates live in both saltwater and freshwater habitats.
source: None of these diverse water dwellers live in both saltwater and freshwater habitats (Evers et al., 2019; Motani and Vermeij, 2021).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations.

claim: Secondarily aquatic vertebrates that live in freshwater habitats have marine antecedents and are all small-bodied.
source: Secondarily aquatic vertebrates that live in freshwater habitats have marine antecedents and are all small-bodied, such as river dolphins (<2.5 m length; Hamilton et al., 2001), small lake-bound seals (<2 m; Fulton and Strobeck, 2010), the river-bound Amazonian manatee (<2.5 m; Guterres-Pazin, 2014), and a few mosasaurs and plesiosaurs of modest body size (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a general statement about freshwater aquatic vertebrates supported by citations.

claim: Large-bodied semiaquatic reptiles frequent coastal and inland locales today and in the past.
source: Large-bodied semiaquatic reptiles, in contrast, frequent coastal and inland locales today and in the past.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about semiaquatic reptiles based on knowledge.

claim: Sarcosuchus imperator, among the largest of semiaquatic reptiles (~12 m length), lived in the same inland basin as S. tenerensis.
source: Sarcosuchus imperator, among the largest of semiaquatic reptiles (~12 m length; Sereno et al., 2001), lived in the same inland basin as S. tenerensis.
evidence: This is a statement about fossil co-occurrence supported by citation.

claim: The fossil record supports the interpretation of Spinosaurus as a semiaquatic bipedal ambush predator that frequented the margins of both coastal and inland waterways.
source: The fossil record supports our interpretation of Spinosaurus as a semiaquatic bipedal ambush predator that frequented the margins of both coastal and inland waterways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fossil distribution data.

claim: The large body size of S. aegyptiacus and older related species such as S. tenerensis mitigates against an aquatic interpretation for the former as it would constitute the only instance among vertebrates where the evolution of a secondarily aquatic species occurred at body size greater than 2–3 m.
source: The large body size of S. aegyptiacus and older related species such as S. tenerensis also mitigates against an aquatic interpretation for the former as it would constitute the only instance among vertebrates where the evolution of a secondarily aquatic species occurred at body size greater than 2–3 m.
evidence: This is an argument based on comparative patterns in vertebrate evolution.

claim: All other large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates evolved the adaptations requisite for an aquatic lifestyle at small body size, increasing in body size once fully established within the marine realm.
source: All other large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates (e.g., ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, metriorhynchoid crocodylomorphs, protostegid turtles, mosasaurs, sirenians, whales) evolved the adaptations requisite for an aquatic lifestyle at small body size, increasing in body size once fully established within the marine realm (Domning, 2000; Thewissen et al., 2009; Polcyn et al., 2014; Moon and Stubbs, 2020; Motani and Vermeij, 2021).
evidence: This is a general statement about the evolution of aquatic vertebrates supported by citations.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of an enlarged dataset for spinosaurids clarifies piscivorous adaptations in the earliest spinosaurids (stage 1, ~130 Ma) that enhance prey capture in shallow water and heighten visual display.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of an enlarged dataset for spinosaurids clarifies piscivorous adaptations in the earliest spinosaurids (stage 1, ~130 Ma) that enhance prey capture in shallow water and heighten visual display (Figure 8; Appendix 5).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Piscivorous adaptations in the earliest spinosaurids include an elongate snout tipped with a dental rosette for snaring fish, retracted external nares to inhibit water intake, and a prominent nasal crest.
source: In the skull, these include an elongate snout tipped with a dental rosette for snaring fish, retracted external nares to inhibit water intake, and a prominent nasal crest (Charig and Milner, 1997; Sereno et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a description of cranial adaptations supported by citations.

claim: The ornamental crest over the snout in the earliest spinosaurids is accompanied by the evolution of a postcranial sail of varying height supported by neural spines of the posterior dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae.
source: The ornamental crest over the snout is accompanied by the evolution of a postcranial sail of varying height supported by neural spines of the posterior dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae (Stromer, 1915; Sereno et al., 1998; Allain et al., 2012; Barker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of postcranial features supported by citations.

claim: The earliest spinosaurids have 'cervicalized' anterior trunk vertebrae to enhance ventroflexion and the effective length of the neck, presumably as an adaptation to feeding in water.
source: The earliest spinosaurids, in addition, have 'cervicalized' anterior trunk vertebrae to enhance ventroflexion and the effective length of the neck, presumably as an adaptation to feeding in water (Hone and Holtz, 2021).
evidence: This is a description of vertebral modifications supported by citation.

claim: Neural spines over the trunk and tail are heightened to varying degrees in all spinosaurids including baryonychines.
source: Neural spines over the trunk and tail are heightened to varying degrees in all spinosaurids including baryonychines (Figure 1F and I).
evidence: This is an observation shown in Figure 1F and I.

claim: Baryonychines have a low, cruciate nasal crest and swollen brow ridges over the orbits for display or agonistic purposes.
source: Baryonychines (e.g., Suchomimus, Baryonyx, Ceratosuchops) have a low, cruciate nasal crest and swollen brow ridges over the orbits for display or agonistic purposes.
evidence: This is a description of baryonychine features with functional interpretation.

claim: Spinosaurines exhibit further specializations for piscivory and display (stage 2).
source: Spinosaurines, on the other hand, exhibit further specializations for piscivory and display (Figures 1A and 8, stage 2).
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary stages shown in Figures 1A and 8.

claim: Piscivorous adaptations in spinosaurines include spaced teeth with smooth carinae for puncturing efficiency, smaller, more retracted external nares to inhibit water intake, more prominent muscle attachments on the ventral aspect of cervicodorsal vertebrae for ventral lunging, and scythe-shaped manual unguals for slicing.
source: Piscivorous adaptations include spaced teeth with smooth carinae for puncturing efficiency, smaller, more retracted external nares to inhibit water intake, more prominent muscle attachments on the ventral aspect of cervicodorsal vertebrae for ventral lunging, and scythe-shaped manual unguals for slicing (Sues et al., 2002; Dal Sasso et al., 2005; Ibrahim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of spinosaurine features supported by citations.

claim: Adaptations for enhanced display in spinosaurines include a heightened cranial crest, low cervical sail, and a hypertrophied torso-to-caudal sail.
source: Adaptations for enhanced display include a heightened cranial crest, low cervical sail, and a hypertrophied torso-to-caudal sail.
evidence: This is a description of display features with functional interpretation.

claim: In 1915 Ernst Stromer highlighted the remarkable adaptations in the jaws and neural spines of S. aegyptiacus for piscivory and ostentatious display, respectively, citing modern analogs for both.
source: In 1915 Ernst Stromer highlighted the remarkable adaptations in the jaws and neural spines of S. aegyptiacus for piscivory and ostentatious display, respectively, citing modern analogs for both (Stromer, 1915).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation.

claim: The unveiling of a new partial skeleton from Morocco and its tail 6 years later generated hypotheses for semiaquatic and aquatic interpretations, respectively.
source: Indeed, the unveiling of a new partial skeleton from Morocco (Ibrahim et al., 2014) and its tail 6 years later (Ibrahim et al., 2020b) generated hypotheses for semiaquatic and aquatic interpretations, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of interpretations supported by citations.

claim: The superficially eel-like morphology of the tail, viewed as a 'novel propulsor organ,' provided the inspiration for the 'aquatic hypothesis'.
source: The superficially eel-like morphology of the tail, viewed as a 'novel propulsor organ,' provided the inspiration for the 'aquatic hypothesis,' which envisioned S. aegyptiacus as a tail-propelled, diving predator 'that pursued and caught its prey in the water column' (Ibrahim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the basis for the aquatic hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: The aquatic hypothesis envisioned S. aegyptiacus as a tail-propelled, diving predator 'that pursued and caught its prey in the water column'.
source: The superficially eel-like morphology of the tail, viewed as a 'novel propulsor organ,' provided the inspiration for the 'aquatic hypothesis,' which envisioned S. aegyptiacus as a tail-propelled, diving predator 'that pursued and caught its prey in the water column' (Ibrahim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the aquatic hypothesis, supported by citation.

claim: The terrestrial capabilities of S. aegyptiacus were regarded as seriously diminished by a trunk-positioned center of body mass that would require a quadrupedal stance on land.
source: Conversely, as would be requisite for status as a secondarily aquatic reptile, its terrestrial capabilities were regarded as seriously diminished by a trunk-positioned center of body mass (Ibrahim et al., 2014; Ibrahim et al., 2020b) that would require a quadrupedal stance on land and the use of long-clawed forelimbs not at all designed for weight support.
evidence: This describes the aquatic hypothesis, supported by citations.

claim: Fabbri et al used bone compactness to assert that S. aegyptiacus was a 'subaqueous forager' with diving bona fides.
source: Presented as support for the aquatic hypothesis, Fabbri et al used bone compactness to assert that S. aegyptiacus was a 'subaqueous forager' with diving bona fides (Fabbri et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes an argument made by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: In order to conclude that S. aegyptiacus was an aquatic diver and pursuit predator, one must understand its buoyancy, stability, velocity, maneuverability, and diving performance in water.
source: In order to conclude that S. aegyptiacus was an aquatic diver and pursuit predator, one also must understand its buoyancy, stability, velocity, maneuverability, and diving performance in water.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for evaluating the aquatic hypothesis.

claim: Major discrepancies exist between the authors' CT-based skeletal model and the original 3D skeletal model and the 2D skeletal silhouette used by the aquatic hypothesis.
source: Therefore, we began with CT scans of the fossils to piece together an accurate skeletal model, discovering major discrepancies with the original 3D skeletal model (Ibrahim et al., 2014) and the 2D skeletal silhouette used by the aquatic hypothesis (Fabbri et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes findings from the skeletal reconstruction, with citations to previous models.

claim: Skeletal regions anterior to the hips are enlarged in length and depth beyond the dimensions of the CT-based reconstruction in the 2D model used by the aquatic hypothesis, shifting the CM in the resulting flesh model forward from the hips to the trunk.
source: Comparisons to the 2D model with the more accurate tail show that skeletal regions anterior to the hips are enlarged in length and depth beyond the dimensions of our CT-based reconstruction, shifting the CM in the resulting flesh model forward from the hips to the trunk.
evidence: This is a result from comparing skeletal reconstructions.

claim: Trunk length was increased in both previous models of S. aegyptiacus due to unnatural ventroflexion of the dorsal column that also spread further the neural spines of the sail.
source: Trunk length was increased in both previous models of S. aegyptiacus due to unnatural ventroflexion of the dorsal column that also spread further the neural spines of the sail (Figure 9).
evidence: This is an observation about previous reconstructions shown in Figure 9.

claim: When neotype or rebuilt holotype dorsal vertebrae of S. aegyptiacus are rearticulated in an osteological neutral pose, the shorter torso has a straighter column with less spread neural spines.
source: When neotype (CT-scanned) or rebuilt holotype dorsal vertebrae of S. aegyptiacus are rearticulatd in an osteological neutral pose, the shorter torso has a straighter column with less spread neural spines.
evidence: This is a result from rearticulating the vertebrae.

claim: The ribcage in S. aegyptiacus is not as deep as in previous reconstructions, based on the preserved rib pieces of the holotype and neotype and the nearly complete ribcage known for S. tenerensis.
source: The ribcage, in addition, is not as deep, based on the preserved rib pieces of the holotype and neotype and the nearly complete ribcage known for S. tenerensis (Figures 1F and 9).
evidence: This is a result from comparing ribcage reconstructions shown in Figures 1F and 9.

claim: The flesh model used by the aquatic hypothesis underestimated the muscle mass at the base of the tail.
source: The flesh model used by the aquatic hypothesis, likewise, underestimated the muscle mass at the base of the tail, judging from our study of CT scans of crocodylians and a range of other reptiles (Díez Díaz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on CT scans of extant reptiles, supported by citation.

claim: S. aegyptiacus failed spectacularly by factors from four- to tenfold for maximum swimming speed on the surface or underwater, for the capacity to right and remain stable or maneuver underwater, and for generating the force needed to overcome buoyancy and fully submerge.
source: S. aegyptiacus failed spectacularly by factors from four- to tenfold for maximum swimming speed on the surface or underwater (Figure 3A), for the capacity to right and remain stable or maneuver underwater (Figure 3B), and for generating the force needed to overcome buoyancy and fully submerge.
evidence: This is a summary of biomechanical results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: S. aegyptiacus was an unstable, slow swimmer without the capacity to submerge.
source: S. aegyptiacus was an unstable, slow swimmer without the capacity to submerge.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the biomechanical analyses.

claim: S. aegyptiacus fails comparative tests when plotted against various extant and extinct secondarily aquatic amniotes for appendage area, the size of foot and tail paddles in crocodylians, tail structure, and the habitats occupied by large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates.
source: We thought of other comparative means to test the aquatic hypothesis, plotting S. aegyptiacus against various extant and extinct secondarily aquatic amniotes to consider appendage area (Figure 5), the size of foot and tail paddles in crocodylians (Figure 6), tail structure (Figure 4C and D), and the habitats occupied by large-bodied secondarily aquatic vertebrates (Figure 7A). S. aegyptiacus fails all of these comparative tests as well because it resembles other theropod dinosaurs in limb size, other reptiles that use midline sails for display, and semiaquatic reptiles in the diversity of coastal and inland habitats occupied.
evidence: This is a summary of comparative results shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: The overall skeletal proportions and form of S. aegyptiacus are largely known.
source: Although additional fossils of S. aegyptiacus and other spinosaurids will surely come to light, the overall skeletal proportions and form of S. aegyptiacus are largely known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The aquatic hypothesis is unlikely to survive as a plausible lifestyle interpretation.
source: The aquatic hypothesis, for that reason, is unlikely to survive as a plausible lifestyle interpretation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analyses presented.

claim: The authors and Hone and Holtz envision S. aegyptiacus as a bipedal, semiaquatic dinosaur using ambush predation of large fish while wading into shallow coastal and riverine waters.
source: What then is our lifestyle interpretation for S. aegyptiacus? Our study and that of Hone and Holtz, 2021 envision S. aegyptiacus as a bipedal, semiaquatic dinosaur using ambush predation of large fish while wading into shallow coastal and riverine waters.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation, supported by citation to similar conclusions.

claim: The composite skeletal reconstruction of S. aegyptiacus is based principally on bones of holotypic and neotypic specimens supplemented by associated and isolated bones from Cenomanian-age formations in Egypt, Morocco, and Niger.
source: The composite skeletal reconstruction of S. aegyptiacus is based principally on bones of holotypic and neotypic specimens supplemented by associated and isolated bones from Cenomanian-age formations in Egypt, Morocco, and Niger (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the data sources for the skeletal reconstruction shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The two most important specimens for the skeletal reconstruction include the subadult partial skeleton composing the holotype from the Western Desert of Egypt and a subadult partial skeleton designated as the neotype from the Kem Kem Group in Morocco.
source: The two most important specimens include the subadult partial skeleton composing the holotype (BSP 9012 VIII 19) from the Western Desert of Egypt (Stromer, 1915; Smith et al., 2006) and a subadult partial skeleton designated as the neotype from the Kem Kem Group in Morocco (FSAC-KK 11888; Ibrahim et al., 2014; Ibrahim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the key specimens used, supported by citations.

claim: All bones of the neotype have been CT-scanned except for recently discovered bones of the tail.
source: Of these three specimens, only the bones of the neotype are preserved, all of which have been CT-scanned except for recently discovered bones of the tail (Ibrahim et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes the data available for the neotype, with citation.

claim: All digital bones were articulated in osteologically neutral pose, a standardizing criterion for comparing vertebrate skeletons.
source: All digital bones were articulated in osteologically neutral pose (Stevens and Parrish, 1999), a standardizing criterion for comparing vertebrate skeletons (Mallison, 2010; Vidal et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the methodology for articulating the skeleton, supported by citations.
